parakeet: If enough people pretend to know things they don't actually understand, we lose something incredibly important. Our ability to solve problems together. Because solving real problems requires experimentation, evidence, humility, and revision. Instead of asking what works, people argue over who's right. And that's how societies get stuck. Because people are more committed to defending their ideas than testing their ideas. When an entire culture adopts this cognitive lethargy, we create a society of performative experts. We stop solving problems and start competing for who can articulate the idea most passionately. In politics and culture, we vote for the most confident person with the biggest idea, even if they've never stepped foot in the lab of execution. This makes us incredibly vulnerable to demagogues and grifters. If we don't value the mechanics of how things work, we can be sold a miracle that's actually just a disaster wrapped in confirmation bias. People become emotionally invested in their solutions long before those solutions have been demonstrated to work, which means they stop asking the most important question of all. Not I believe this, but have I tried to understand this? Not this sounds right, but has this been demonstrated? Because the real opposite of superstition isn't atheism. The real opposite of superstition is intellectual responsibility. And that responsibility starts with a simple principle. No matter how confident someone sounds, your certainty should never come from their confidence. It should come from your comprehension, your understanding. Truth doesn't demand confidence, it survives experimentation. And if we want to build a better world beyond superstition, we have to stop pretending we know things and start actually trying to know them.
